lessons.title: Brahman and the Three Features of the Divine
lessons.overall_verdict: PASS — no substantive errors; one citation notation issue

issues.category: Upanishad citation — non-standard reference format
issues.quoted_text: The three features of the divine (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 391): (1) everywhere as non-personal Brahman; (2) within the heart; (3) beyond, as a personal loving God.
issues.problem: The reference '391' is a page number from Patrick Olivelle's Oxford World's Classics translation (1996), not a chapter-and-verse citation in the conventional scholarly format. The passage is more standardly cited as Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.3 (the 'two forms of Brahman' section) for the nirguna/saguna distinction, and 3.7 for 'the inner controller' (antaryamin) as the divine within. Critically, '391' is the exact reference reproduced in the AQA 8062 specification itself, so using it here is consistent with how examiners expect students to cite it — this is not an error for GCSE purposes. It is flagged only so content editors know the '391' is a translation page reference, not a chapter/verse, should it ever be queried.
issues.correction: No change needed for GCSE audience. If adding a scholarly note, clarify: 'Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 391 (Olivelle translation, 1996), broadly corresponding to BrUp 2.3 and 3.7.'

issues.category: Advaita Vedanta — Shankara dating
issues.location: Section: Nirguna and Saguna in Different Sub-Traditions
issues.quoted_text: The Advaita Vedanta school, associated with the philosopher Shankara (8th century CE)
issues.problem: The scholarly consensus dates Shankara to c. 700–750 CE, making '8th century CE' correct. Traditional Hindu monasteries (mathas) date him to c. 509–477 BCE. For GCSE, '8th century CE' is the accepted scholarly dating and is correct.
issues.correction: No change needed. '8th century CE' is the scholarly-accepted date.

lessons.title: The Tri-murti, Deities and Avatars
lessons.overall_verdict: PASS — concepts accurate; one minor citation issue with Rig Veda cosmology reference

issues.category: Rig Veda cosmology citation — verse range
issues.location: Section: Matter, the Three Qualities and Illusion
issues.quoted_text: Hindu cosmology (Rig Veda 10.129.6–7) describes the universe as emerging from a primordial state of undifferentiation, with creation and dissolution cycling endlessly through four ages (yugas).
issues.problem: Rig Veda 10.129 (Nasadiya Sukta) is the Creation Hymn — its verses 6–7 specifically concern the epistemological uncertainty of creation's origins ('who really knows?'), not the cycling of four yugas (Satya, Treta, Dvapara, Kali). The yuga cosmology originates in the Puranas (especially Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana), not in the Nasadiya Sukta. The lesson conflates two separate concepts under one citation. RV 10.129 is correctly invoked for the 'primordial undifferentiation' aspect, but the yuga cycling should not be attributed to it.
issues.correction: Split the claim: 'The Nasadiya Sukta (Rig Veda 10.129) describes the universe as emerging from a primordial state of undifferentiation. Later Puranic cosmology teaches that creation and dissolution cycle endlessly through four ages (yugas).'

issues.category: Tri-murti — Brahma temples claim
issues.quoted_text: dedicated temples to Brahma alone are rare (the Brahma Temple at Pushkar in Rajasthan is one of the most famous)
issues.problem: Correct. The Brahma Temple at Pushkar is widely cited as the only major temple dedicated to Brahma in India. The claim that such temples are rare is accurate and well-established.
issues.correction: No change needed.

lessons.title: Atman, Samsara, Karma and Moksha
lessons.overall_verdict: PASS — strong and accurate; concepts well-differentiated by school

issues.category: Bhagavad Gita description of atman — paraphrase not flagged
issues.quoted_text: The Bhagavad Gita describes the atman as indestructible: it cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, wetted by water or dried by wind.
issues.problem: This accurately paraphrases BG 2.23–2.24, which is the correct locus for this teaching. The paraphrase is conceptually sound. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed. A verse citation (BG 2.23–24) would strengthen the passage but is not required at GCSE level.

issues.category: Vishishtadvaita — Ramanuja summary
issues.quoted_text: In Vishishtadvaita (associated with Ramanuja), atman is real but distinct from God — the individual soul is a part of Brahman, as the body is a part of the self.
issues.problem: Accurate and well-expressed. Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita does teach that souls and matter form the 'body' of Brahman while retaining their real individual identity. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

lessons.title: The Four Aims of Life and Dharma
lessons.overall_verdict: PASS — accurate throughout; no significant errors

issues.category: Kama Sutra description — accurate but could invite misreading
issues.quoted_text: The famous Hindu text the Kama Sutra is not simply about sexual practice, as it is often misunderstood in the West; it is a broad guide to pleasure and the arts of living well.
issues.problem: Correct clarification. The Kama Sutra (Vatsyayana, c. 2nd–4th century CE) does cover aesthetics, social conduct and the arts of life, not only sexual technique. The lesson handles this with appropriate nuance for a 15–16 year old GCSE audience.
issues.correction: No change needed.

issues.category: Bhagavad Gita and dharma — Arjuna narrative accurate
issues.quoted_text: When the warrior Arjuna hesitates to fight because he sees his relatives on the opposing side, Krishna teaches him that his dharma as a warrior requires him to fight righteously.
issues.problem: Correct summary of BG 1–2. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

lessons.title: Worship at Home and the Mandir
lessons.overall_verdict: FAIL — HIGH severity factual error on Neasden Temple construction materials

issues.category: Wrong construction material — Neasden Temple
issues.location: Key Fact box on the Mandir
issues.quoted_text: It was built entirely from hand-carved Turkish limestone and Italian marble, without the use of steel, following ancient Vedic Shilpa Shastra building principles.
issues.problem: The limestone used in the Neasden BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir is Bulgarian limestone, not Turkish. The official BAPS Mandir website and Wikipedia both confirm: 5,000 tonnes of Bulgarian limestone were shipped to Rajasthan where over 1,500 sculptors carved it over three years, then the 26,300 numbered pieces were assembled in London. Turkish limestone is associated with other BAPS mandirs (e.g. Chicago, Stafford) but not Neasden. The marble reference to 'Italian' is partially correct — some Carrara marble from Italy was used for load-bearing columns and flooring — but Ambaji marble from Gujarat (India) was also used. The lesson's sweeping 'Italian marble' also undersells the Indian sourcing. The steel claim ('without the use of steel') is correct.
issues.correction: Change to: 'It was built entirely from hand-carved Bulgarian limestone and marble (including Ambaji marble from India and Carrara marble from Italy), without the use of steel, following ancient Vedic Shilpa Shastra building principles.'

issues.category: Outdated superlative claim — 'largest Hindu temple outside India'
issues.location: Body text and Key Fact box
issues.quoted_text: the largest Hindu temple outside India
issues.problem: The Neasden Temple held the Guinness World Record as the largest traditionally built Hindu temple outside India at its completion in 1995 and official certification in 2000. Since then, larger BAPS mandirs have been built (notably in Robbinsville, New Jersey, USA — the BAPS Swaminarayan Akshardham, completed 2023, is now the world's largest Hindu temple overall). The claim as written is no longer accurate. For British context, Neasden remains the largest in Europe, but 'outside India' is now incorrect.
issues.correction: Change to: 'the largest Hindu temple in Europe' (or add a qualifier: 'at the time of its completion, the largest Hindu temple outside India').

issues.category: Arati dish description
issues.quoted_text: the waving of a flame (typically in a multi-wicked lamp called a thali or aarti dish)
issues.problem: A thali is technically a flat plate or tray (the broader vessel used in puja), not specifically the name for the arati lamp. The arati lamp itself is more precisely called a 'diya' (single wick), 'pancha-diya' or 'pancha-pradeep' (five-wicked), or simply 'aarti diya/aarti lamp'. Calling it a 'thali' is loose but widely used colloquially to describe the puja tray that holds the lamp. This is a LOW issue — not technically wrong in everyday usage but could confuse students who learn 'thali' means a meal platter.
issues.correction: Consider: 'waving of a flame (typically held in a multi-wicked lamp, often placed on a puja tray called a thali)'.

lessons.title: Focuses of Worship and the Murti
lessons.overall_verdict: PASS — accurate; scripture quotation requires a source note

issues.category: Rig Veda 1.164.46 — translation variant
issues.quoted_text: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names (Rig Veda 1.164.46)
issues.problem: The verse citation is correct (RV 1.164.46, the Dirghatamas hymn). The standard scholarly translation of 'ekam sat viprā bahudhā vadanti' is 'Truth/Being is one; sages call it by many names' — 'vipra' means 'sages/inspired seers', not 'the wise' generically. The lesson's rendering 'the wise' is a common popular paraphrase and is conceptually accurate, but technically 'sages' or 'seers' would be more precise. No factual error, but the paraphrase softens the Vedic voice.
issues.correction: Optional precision improvement: 'Truth is one; the sages call it by many names (Rig Veda 1.164.46).'

issues.category: Bhagavad Gita 4.11 — quotation attribution
issues.location: Section: Focuses of Worship — Personal vs Non-Personal
issues.quoted_text: In whatever way people are devoted to me, in that same way I fulfil their desires.
issues.problem: This is a paraphrase of BG 4.11 ('ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃs tathaiva bhajāmy aham'). The lesson does not cite the verse number. The concept is accurately represented. The verse actually means 'In whatever way people surrender/approach Me, I reciprocate accordingly' — not exactly 'fulfil their desires' (which could imply wish-granting). The correct sense is that God meets devotees on their own terms and path. LOW issue — conceptually close but 'fulfil their desires' slightly misrepresents the meaning of 'bhajāmy'.
issues.correction: Rephrase as: 'In whatever way people surrender to me, I respond accordingly (Bhagavad Gita 4.11)' and add the verse citation.

issues.category: Guru verse — Sanskrit attribution
issues.quoted_text: Guru Brahma, Guru Vishnu, Guru Devo Maheshwara
issues.problem: This verse ('Gurur Brahma Gurur Vishnu Gurur Devo Maheshvara / Gurur Sakshat Para Brahma Tasmai Shri Gurave Namah') is from the Guru Stotram, a devotional hymn attributed to Adi Shankaracharya and found in the Skanda Purana. It is not from the primary Vedic canon. The lesson presents it correctly as a 'well-known Sanskrit verse' without over-claiming its canonical status. No factual error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

lessons.title: Festivals: Diwali and Holi
lessons.overall_verdict: PASS — festival content accurate and well-sourced; one structural note on Diwali day 4

issues.category: Diwali Day 4 — Govardhan Puja location detail omitted
issues.location: Section: The Five Days of Diwali — Day 4
issues.quoted_text: Day 4 (Govardhan Puja / Padwa) — associated with Krishna lifting the Govardhan hill; celebrations of new year in some regions.
issues.problem: Correct at GCSE level. For completeness: the Govardhan Hill story specifically involves Krishna protecting the people of Gokul and Vrindavan (in the Braj region), not Mathura city itself — though the broader Mathura district encompasses this area. The lesson does not name a location for this episode, which is the right choice at GCSE level, as the story is widely told without a city-level specification. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

issues.category: Holi origin — Hiranyakashipu's relationship to Holika
issues.quoted_text: Holika (the demon king's sister) tried to burn Prahlada in a fire
issues.problem: Correct. Holika is Hiranyakashipu's sister and Prahlada's aunt. The lesson accurately states the relationship and the theological meaning.
issues.correction: No change needed.

issues.category: Diwali — 'largest Diwali parade outside Asia' — Leicester claim
issues.location: Section: Diwali in Great Britain Today
issues.quoted_text: one of the largest Diwali parades outside Asia
issues.problem: The qualification 'one of the largest' is appropriately hedged. The Leicester Diwali on Belgrave Road (Golden Mile) is routinely cited as the largest Diwali celebration outside India/Asia; 'outside Asia' is the stricter formulation used by some sources. This is consistent with evidence. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

lessons.title: The Four Yogas, Pilgrimage and Hindu Charities
lessons.overall_verdict: FAIL — MEDIUM severity: Key Fact box uses 'astanga yoga' correctly but body text introduces 'raja yoga' equivalence without flagging it is an alternate name, and the Bhagavad Gita 12 quotation is a loose paraphrase presented as direct speech

issues.category: Bhagavad Gita 12 quote — loose paraphrase presented as direct speech
issues.location: Section: Bhakti Yoga: The Path of Devotion
issues.quoted_text: Those who fix their minds on me and worship me with constant devotion — I consider them to be the best yogis.
issues.problem: The lesson presents this as a direct quotation from Bhagavad Gita chapter 12 (verse 2). The actual BG 12.2 reads: 'Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me, ever steadfast and endowed with supreme faith — they are considered by Me to be the most perfect in yoga (yuktatamāh).' The lesson's rendering introduces 'constant devotion' which is not in the original — the verse says 'steadfast' faith (parayā śraddhayā) and 'always engaged' (nitya-yuktāh). More importantly, 'best yogis' is a valid rendering of 'yuktatamāh' (most perfect/best established in yoga), so the core meaning is preserved. However, the framing 'Those who... with constant devotion' conflates the conditions across multiple verses (12.1–2). This is a MEDIUM issue because the quote is presented with quotation marks as if verbatim, when it is a paraphrase.
issues.correction: Either (a) cite as a paraphrase: 'Bhagavad Gita chapter 12 teaches that those who fix their minds on God and worship with steadfast faith are considered the most perfect yogis (BG 12.2).' or (b) use a recognised translation directly.

issues.category: BG 2:47 Edwin Arnold translation — unattributed specific translation
issues.location: Section: Hindu Theology of Service — Karma Yoga as Social Action
issues.quoted_text: Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
issues.problem: This exact phrasing is from Edwin Arnold's 1885 poetic translation 'The Song Celestial' (BG 2.47), not a standard modern scholarly translation. Most current translations render 2.47 as 'You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions' (Prabhupada) or 'Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit thereof' (Arnold). The Arnold version is the source. The lesson presents this as a straightforward Gita quote without indicating it is a particular (19th-century poetic) translation. For GCSE purposes this is an acceptable literary usage, but the archaic 'thy' is distinctive enough that students quoting it in exams should know it is one translator's version.
issues.correction: Add translator attribution or use a more recent rendering: 'The Bhagavad Gita (2.47) teaches: perform your duty without attachment to its fruits' and paraphrase rather than quote Arnold directly.

issues.category: Four yogas Key Fact — 'astanga yoga' correctly used; 'raja yoga' equivalence note
issues.quoted_text: Four yogas: karma yoga (action), jnana yoga (knowledge), astanga yoga (meditation), bhakti yoga (devotion). All lead to moksha. Primary source: the Bhagavad Gita.
issues.problem: The AQA 8062 specification lists the four yogas as karma, jnana, astanga and bhakti — the lesson's Key Fact box matches this exactly. Correct. The lesson body text also correctly introduces 'raja yoga' as an alternative name for astanga yoga (they refer to the same Patanjali system). The equivalence is accurate. However, stating 'Primary source: the Bhagavad Gita' for astanga yoga is slightly misleading — the Bhagavad Gita primarily covers karma, jnana and bhakti yoga (chapters 3, 4 and 12 respectively); astanga yoga as an eight-limbed system is the contribution of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (a separate text from the Gita). The Gita does discuss meditation in chapter 6, but the full astanga framework is Patanjali's.
issues.correction: Adjust to: 'Primary sources: the Bhagavad Gita (karma, jnana, bhakti yoga) and the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (astanga yoga).'

issues.category: Taraka mantra at Varanasi — tradition correctly described
issues.quoted_text: Shiva himself is said to whisper the 'liberation mantra' (taraka mantra) in the ear of the dying.
issues.problem: Correct per Hindu tradition. The taraka mantra belief is attested in the Kashi Khanda of the Skanda Purana and is a standard teaching of Vaishnavite and Shaivite traditions regarding Varanasi. The taraka mantra is traditionally identified as 'Ram Nam' (the name of Rama). The lesson attributes the belief accurately as 'said to' (properly hedging it as tradition) and correctly names the taraka mantra. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

issues.category: Char Dham — four sites correctly named
issues.location: Key Fact box on Char Dham
issues.quoted_text: The Char Dham ('four abodes') are four sacred pilgrimage sites in India — Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameshwaram
issues.problem: Correct. These are the four Bada Char Dham sites traditionally associated with the four cardinal directions. Note: there is a separate 'Chota Char Dham' in the Himalayas (Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath, Badrinath). The lesson's use of 'Char Dham' without qualification refers to the correct four pan-India sites. No error.
issues.correction: No change needed.

summary.overall_quality: Good — 6 of 8 lessons are substantially accurate. One HIGH error (Neasden limestone), one MEDIUM error (outdated 'largest outside India' superlative), two MEDIUM issues (Gita 12.2 paraphrase as direct quote; Arnold translation unattributed). Remaining issues are LOW — translation variations, citation precision, or minor pedagogical refinements.

top_3_worst_lessons.lesson: Worship at Home and the Mandir (384d8d12)
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Contains the only HIGH severity factual error in the set: 'Turkish limestone' is wrong — the Neasden Temple was built from Bulgarian limestone. Also carries a MEDIUM issue: 'largest Hindu temple outside India' is no longer true (surpassed by BAPS Akshardham, Robbinsville, NJ, completed 2023).

top_3_worst_lessons.lesson: The Four Yogas, Pilgrimage and Hindu Charities (70bc0f68)
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Two MEDIUM issues: (1) Bhagavad Gita chapter 12 quote presented in quotation marks as verbatim but contains the word 'constant' not found in the original, and uses a non-standard paraphrase structure. (2) BG 2:47 presented without attribution to Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation — students quoting the archaic 'thy' form in exams without knowing its source may be marked down. Also flags the 'Primary source: the Bhagavad Gita' claim for astanga yoga which should include the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali.

The Rig Veda 10.129.6–7 citation conflates the Nasadiya Sukta (which covers the unknowability of creation's origins) with the yuga cycling cosmology (which originates in Puranic literature, not the Rig Veda). This is a LOW issue but is the most likely scripture citation students would use incorrectly in exam answers if the conflation is not corrected.
